records.question: Which plays must the new check treat as build plays, whose inputs may never name the evals folder? (Q-builders-1)
records.answer: Every play, skill and agent that builds the software, and every context sub-agent it starts, is a build play for the check. Only /shape-slice (which writes the hidden file into the evals folder), /shape-eval and the eval itself may name the evals folder.

trace.asked: who may read the plan evals folder
trace.found: no builder, no skill that builds the software and no context sub-agent reads that folder

source.text: Write the eval that checks, from the outside, that a business intent is met on its slice's surface. The eval is written before the build, from what the plan wrote: the epic, its stories and the slice's hidden file. It never reads an ICE page itself: each line of an ICE has one reader, /shape-slice for the "Fails if" lines and the plan play for the rest (ontology v11, ADR 052). The eval is kept in the plan's evals folder, and no builder, no skill that builds the software and no context sub-agent reads that folder. It matters because a builder that sees the test can build to the test, and then a pass proves nothing.

# Capability: Write the hidden eval

## Directional intent
Write the eval that checks, from the outside, that a business intent is met on its slice's surface. The eval is written before the build, from what the plan wrote: the epic, its stories and the slice's hidden file. source.text: /shape-slice <intent> reads the business intent and the product model, asks the person only what the model and memory do not answer, and writes one slice into the spine with its link to the intent. It also writes the slice's hidden file (failure-and-recovery.md, one entry for each feature) in the plan's evals folder, and a thin ICE for each part the slice needs that has no ICE (ontology v11, ADR 052). It writes no plan, no epic, no story and no eval. Built in #795. Not built yet: the hidden file and the thin ICE need the play's /edit-play change (#842).

  feature needs to be dropped with reason. dont reweite 828."). Everything (ICE, constraints, the model) is plain text; the
  goal is not to hide the eval. "Once the slice happens, we need an eval, and that eval is what we need to pass ... when
  the agents are building, they don't only think through the evals, but they look at the intent and build for that."

# Agents design a named piece of work

**Outcome:** The product owner names a piece of work. Agents shape it into a slice that one person can test, make its plan and write its eval. The product owner confirms each part as it is made.

**Why:** Today the product owner must guide each step of the design by hand. No play designs the work for Garura's own work: the product owner found this while #760 started. When agents do the design, the work is faster and it stays inside its design.

epic's feature-to-story map tells the eval play which story each entry is for.

the evals folder out of the contract".

Where the hidden list, the tests folder or a check is the very thing the feature builds (fn-795 writes the hidden file; fn-898 builds the lint check and the ledger check), a fix given to the builder names it as that product, because it is what the builder sees and changes in the product. source.text: Write the eval that checks, from the outside, that a business intent is met on its slice's surface. The eval is written before the build, from what the plan wrote: the epic, its stories and the slice's hidden file. It never reads an ICE page itself: each line of an ICE has one reader, /shape-slice for the "Fails if" lines and the plan play for the rest (ontology v11, ADR 052). The eval is kept in the plan's evals folder, and no builder, no skill that builds the software and no context sub-agent reads that folder. It matters because a builder that sees the test can build to the test, and then a pass proves nothing.

- Each of the three plays ends at one confirmation by the product owner.
- A play runs each step. No step is done by hand.
- The eval is kept in a place where no builder can read it.

Do not include the design, build, test or validation of an epic (#819), the release plays or /learn-outcomes, or the upgrade of an older product model (#835).
